blocks.s: 3. Careful meditation comes near, then, and does not stay outside, does not cling to the surface, but plants its foot further in. It enters the inward parts, searches each thing; it notes attentively that he did not say, Blessed are the clean of body, but of heart: because it is not enough to keep the hands innocent of evil deeds unless we are cleansed in the mind of wicked thoughts. This the authority of the prophet confirms, who says: Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and the clean of heart (Psalm 23:3-4). Again it considers how much the same prophet longed for this cleanness of heart, who said in prayer, Create a clean heart in me, O God (Psalm 50:12); and again, If I have looked at iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me (Psalm 65:18). It thinks how anxious the blessed Job was in this guard, who said: I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin (Job 31:1). See how strictly the holy man bound himself, who shut his eyes lest he see vanity, lest perhaps he should look unguardedly on what afterwards he would desire against his will. After it has gone through these and similar things about cleanness of heart, it begins to think of its reward: how glorious and delightful it is to see the longed-for face of the Lord, beautiful above the sons of men; no longer cast down and mean, no longer wearing the appearance his mother the Synagogue clothed him in, but robed in the stole of immortality and crowned with the diadem with which his Father crowned him on the day of the resurrection and of glory, the day which the Lord has made. It thinks that in that vision will be the fullness of which the prophet says: I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear (Psalm 16:15). Do you see how much juice has flowed from the smallest grape; how great a fire has risen from this spark; how far this little lump, Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8), has been drawn out on the anvil of meditation? And how much further still it could be drawn, if someone came to it who had lived such things? For I feel that the well is deep; but I am still a raw recruit, and have hardly found what little I have drawn here.

4. Set alight by these torches, stirred by these desires, the soul, the alabaster broken, begins to sense the sweetness of the ointment, not yet by taste but as if by the scent in the nostrils. From this it gathers how sweet it would be to feel the experience of this cleanness, whose mere meditation it has found so pleasant. But what will it do? It burns with the desire to possess, but does not find within itself how it may possess; and the more it seeks, the more it thirsts. As it applies meditation, it applies sorrow too, because it thirsts for the sweetness which meditation shows to be in cleanness of heart, but does not yet taste it. For it is not in the power of the one who reads and meditates to feel this sweetness, unless it is given from above. To read and to meditate is common to the good and the bad alike. Even the philosophers of the nations found, under the guidance of reason, where the highest true good consists; but because, when they had known God, they did not glorify him as God (Romans 1:21), and, presuming on their own powers, said, We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own: who is Lord over us? (Psalm 11:5), they did not deserve to perceive what they were able to see. They became vain in their thoughts (Romans 1:21), and all their wisdom was swallowed up (Psalm 106:27), the wisdom that the study of human learning had brought them, not the Spirit of wisdom, who alone gives true wisdom: that is, savoured knowledge, which gladdens and refreshes with an inestimable savour the soul it has cleaved to. Of that wisdom it is said: Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul (Wisdom 1:4). And this comes from God alone. The Lord granted the office of baptising to many; but the power and authority of forgiving sins in Baptism he kept to himself alone. So John said of him, by way of distinction and as his own name: He it is that baptiseth (John 1:33). In the same way we can say of him: He it is that gives the savour of wisdom and makes the soul savoured. Speech is given to many, but wisdom to few; and the Lord distributes it to whom he will, and as he will.
